senses.definition: Tangled up with something so tightly that the two can no longer act separately.
senses.caution: It is not a neutral word for coupling. It comes out of family therapy and carries a judgement about lost boundaries, so calling two teams enmeshed says their relationship is unhealthy rather than close, and said about actual people it lands like a diagnosis you are not qualified to hand out. If all you mean is that two systems depend on each other, tightly coupled costs you nothing and starts no arguments.
senses.example: Support and engineering aren't collaborating, they're enmeshed - neither one can plan a quarter without the other in the room.

cues.text: You are describing a friend whose life has folded so completely into their partner's that they no longer seem to hold separate opinions about anything.
A cousin's business and their marriage have grown into each other to the point that neither can be sorted out without the other, and you want one word that is honest about the trouble in it.
Two teams can no longer plan a quarter, hire or ship without the other in the room, and you want a word that signals this has gone past healthy collaboration.

You are writing about a supplier relationship where your processes and theirs have grown together so far that leaving would mean rebuilding the business, and you need something stronger than dependent.

distractors: Present in scattered, isolated places rather than across the whole.
Open to something without having agreed to it yet.
Safe to run more than once, because repeat runs change nothing.
An isolated environment where something runs without being able to affect anything real.
A people scattered from a homeland who keep a tie to it, and the fact of that scattering.
